pages.text: Every dawn, Kofiga and his younger sister Enam crossed a quiet arm of Lake Volta to sell fish at the landing beach. They both wore life jackets, always. “The lake gives,” their uncle Nyameye said, “and the lake demands respect.”
sentences: Every dawn, Kofiga and his younger sister Enam crossed a quiet arm of Lake Volta to sell fish at the landing beach.
They both wore life jackets, always.
“The lake gives,” their uncle Nyameye said, “and the lake demands respect.”
pages.alt: Two children in orange life jackets paddle a canoe across calm water at dawn.

pages.text: That morning, a thick fog rolled in. In minutes, they could not see the shore. “Fog forms when cool air meets warmer water,” said Kofiga, remembering his science class. “It will lift when the sun warms the air.” “When?” asked Enam. He did not know.
sentences: That morning, a thick fog rolled in.
In minutes, they could not see the shore.
“Fog forms when cool air meets warmer water,” said Kofiga, remembering his science class.
“It will lift when the sun warms the air.” “When?” asked Enam.
He did not know.
pages.alt: The canoe sits in thick white fog with no shore in sight.

pages.text: Then, a soft blue light appeared on the water ahead, floating, drifting, as if someone carried a lantern. Enam gasped. “Is it a boat?” “Or the lake spirit,” whispered Kofiga. Old fishermen told stories of a light that leads boats away, or home.
sentences: Then, a soft blue light appeared on the water ahead, floating, drifting, as if someone carried a lantern.
Enam gasped.
“Is it a boat?” “Or the lake spirit,” whispered Kofiga.
Old fishermen told stories of a light that leads boats away, or home.
pages.alt: A faint blue lantern-like glow floats in the fog ahead of the canoe.

pages.text: The light moved slowly, as if to say follow me. Kofiga stopped paddling. “Rule one,” he said. “We do not follow something we do not understand.” He turned the canoe against the light’s direction. “Rule two: we use what we know.”
sentences: The light moved slowly, as if to say follow me.
Kofiga stopped paddling.
“Rule one,” he said.
“We do not follow something we do not understand.” He turned the canoe against the light’s direction.
“Rule two: we use what we know.”
pages.alt: A boy holds his paddle still and points the canoe away from the glowing light.

pages.text: They stopped the motor and listened. Faint sounds came from one direction: a rooster crowing, a dog barking, the clang of a bell. “Sounds travel over water,” said Kofiga. “The village is that way.” Enam tied the lamp to the bow and blew her whistle in short bursts.
sentences: They stopped the motor and listened.
Faint sounds came from one direction: a rooster crowing, a dog barking, the clang of a bell.
“Sounds travel over water,” said Kofiga.
“The village is that way.” Enam tied the lamp to the bow and blew her whistle in short bursts.
pages.alt: The children listen in the fog while one blows a whistle and a lamp shines at the bow.

pages.text: Slowly, they paddled towards the sounds, keeping low in the canoe. The blue light drifted beside them, never closer, never farther. Enam shivered. “It is not leading us,” said Kofiga. “It is only with us.” For the first time, the light did not feel scary. It felt like company.
sentences: Slowly, they paddled towards the sounds, keeping low in the canoe.
The blue light drifted beside them, never closer, never farther.
Enam shivered.
“It is not leading us,” said Kofiga.
“It is only with us.” For the first time, the light did not feel scary.
It felt like company.
pages.alt: The canoe moves slowly through fog with the blue light drifting beside it.

pages.text: Then a voice boomed across the water: “Kofiga! Enam!” Uncle Nyameye’s lamp swung back and forth on the shore. The sun broke through, and the fog lifted like a curtain. They landed safely on the beach. Their uncle hugged them both. “You waited, listened and used your heads,” he said.
sentences: Then a voice boomed across the water: “Kofiga!
Enam!” Uncle Nyameye’s lamp swung back and forth on the shore.
The sun broke through, and the fog lifted like a curtain.
They landed safely on the beach.
Their uncle hugged them both.
“You waited, listened and used your heads,” he said.
pages.alt: The canoe reaches a beach where an uncle with a lamp waits and the fog is clearing.

pages.text: Kofiga looked back at the lake. The blue light was still there, hovering above the water, brighter than before. Then it dipped, like a bow, and was gone. “Marsh gas?” guessed Enam. “Or a fisherman’s lamp, or a spirit.” “Or all three,” said Uncle Nyameye. “A good fisher respects the lake and never follows a light into fog.” The end.
sentences: Kofiga looked back at the lake.

pages.alt: The glowing light dips like a bow over the lake as the sun rises over a clear horizon.
